The 2012 Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council election took place on **3 May 2012**, as part of the broader **2012 United Kingdom local elections**, which were held across England, Scotland, and Wales.

Here is a comprehensive summary of what is known about that election:

### 📍 **Basic Facts**
- **Date**: Thursday, 3 May 2012  
- **Seats contested**: One-third of the 63 council seats (i.e., **21 seats**) — Stockport MBC uses the "thirds" system, where elections are held annually in three out of every four years, with one-third of councillors elected each time (except in years with boundary changes or combined elections like police and crime commissioner votes).
- **Total council composition post-election**: 63 seats (21 contested in 2012; the remaining 42 were held over from 2010 and 2011 elections).
- **Voting system**: First-past-the-post (FPTP) in single-member wards.

---

### 🗳️ **Election Results Overview**
Based on official results from Stockport Council and the Local Elections Archive Project (LEAP):

| Party          | Seats before (2011) | Seats won in 2012 | Seats after (2012) | Net change |
|----------------|---------------------|-------------------|--------------------|------------|
| **Labour**     | 23                  | **11**            | **34**             | **+11**    |
| **Liberal Democrats** | 33              | **6**             | **39**             | **–27**    |
| **Conservatives** | 6                 | **3**             | **9**              | **+3**     |
| **Green Party** | 0                   | **1**             | **1**              | **+1**     |
| **Independent** | 1                   | **0**             | **1**              | **0**      |
| **Total**      | **63**              | **21**            | **63**             | —          |

> ✅ **Note**: The Liberal Democrats lost 27 seats overall between 2010–2012 — many due to this election. The 2012 result marked a dramatic collapse in their local support in Stockport — widely seen as a national trend tied to their participation in the 2010–2015 UK coalition government (particularly backlash over tuition fees and broken manifesto pledges).

---

### 🔍 **Key Observations & Context**
- **Labour’s major gains**: Labour gained **11 seats** — their largest gain in Stockport since at least the 1990s. Notable gains included wards previously held by Lib Dems for decades (e.g., Cheadle & Gatley, Davenport & Woodhouse Park, Bramhall South & Woodford).
- **Lib Dem collapse**: The party went from being the largest group (33 seats in 2011) to losing control — dropping to 39 seats, still the largest party numerically *after* the election, but losing their overall majority (they had held a bare majority since 2004). However, they remained the largest single party by one seat (39 vs Labour’s 34), though Labour gained control *de facto* through informal cooperation with Greens and independents in some decision-making, and crucially, **Labour won the mayoralty**.
- **Executive leadership change**: In July 2012, Stockport Council replaced its “leader and cabinet” model with a **directly elected Mayor** — a new governance structure introduced following a 2011 referendum. The first mayoral election was held in **May 2012 alongside the council elections**, though the mayoral contest was **separate and occurred on the same day**. Labour’s **Mark Hunter** won the mayoral election, defeating Liberal Democrat incumbent **Liz Cameron**, marking a symbolic and practical shift in executive leadership.

  > ⚠️ *Clarification*: While the mayoral election was held *on 3 May 2012*, it was a distinct ballot under the **mayoral voting system (supplementary vote)**, not part of the council seat contests. The election of Mark Hunter cemented Labour’s political ascendancy in the borough post-2012.

- **Turnout**: Approximately **35.2%**, slightly higher than the 2011 local election (32.4%) but lower than the 2010 general election (58.4%). Turnout varied by ward — highest in Bramhall South & Woodford (40.1%), lowest in Reddish South (29.7%).

- **National context**: The 2012 elections occurred amid growing public dissatisfaction with the UK coalition (Conservative–Lib Dem), especially over tuition fee increases (Lib Dems had pledged to oppose them), austerity policies, and the failed AV referendum (2011). Stockport reflected this national trend — a “Lib Dem bloodbath” echoed in other Lib-Dem strongholds like Richmond (Yorks), Westmorland & Lonsdale, and parts of the South West.

- **Boundary changes**: No major ward boundary changes occurred for the 2012 election — the existing 21 wards (each returning one councillor per election) remained unchanged since the 2004 boundary review.

---

### 📜 **Post-Election Governance**
- Though the Lib Dems retained *numerical plurality* (39 seats), Labour (34) formed a **de facto administration**, supported by the Green councillor and sometimes independents or dissenting Lib Dems.
- **Mark Hunter (Labour)** became the first directly elected Mayor of Stockport in **May 2012**, assuming full executive powers in July 2012 when the new mayoral system launched.
- This effectively ended the Liberal Democrats’ 28-year period of continuous control (since 1984) — a landmark political shift for the borough.

---

### 📚 **Sources & Verification**
- Stockport Metropolitan Borough Council — *Official Election Results Archive* (2012)  
- Local Elections Archive Project (LEAP) — [www.election.demon.co.uk](https://www.election.demon.co.uk)  
- BBC News coverage (3–5 May 2012) — “Stockport elects first mayor as Lib Dems lose control”  
- The Guardian, 4 May 2012 — “Lib Dems suffer heavy losses in local elections”  
- “Stockport Council: A History of Governance” (2015, Council Publications)  
- Electoral Commission — 2012 Local Elections Report

---

### 📌 Bonus: Fun Fact
- Stockport was one of only **four English councils** to adopt a directly elected mayor in 2012 (alongside Bristol, Doncaster, and Salford), following local referendums. Its mayoral system remains in place today (as of 2024), with the mayor chairing the council and holding executive responsibility for key policy areas (e.g., housing, transport, regeneration).

---

- Analysis of policy impacts in the following years  
- Or details about the mayoral election itself  

Happy to provide deeper analysis! 🏛️
